In this module we will extend our work with spatial vector data by learning how to manage the memory required by large and complex geometries. We will also take our first steps into working with raster data! Specifically, you will learn:

* How to manage the memory allocation of a session
* The *terra* package -- the new(ish) package for working with raster data in R.

*Note: Please continue to ignore references to the folder structure from our data science class.*

## Module overview

* **5.2 Memory management and shapefiles**: In this lesson we will review some of our core shapefile tools while learning how to avoid dreaded out-of-memory errors when working with shapefiles.
* **5.3 Introduction to raster data**: In this video lesson (runtime: 47:04) and brief written tutorial, we will review what raster files are and how to use the *terra* package for reading in raster data, raster pre-processing, and data extraction.

**Problem Set** (due 28 Sep): Community science

## Getting started

Please complete the following steps *prior* to beginning this week's lessons:

* Download [module_5_files.zip]{.mono} and:
    * Place the [rasters]{.mono} folder in [data/raw]{.mono}. *Note: Please place the folder itself in that location, not the data within the folder. Additionally, please do not change the name of the folder!*
    * Place any [\*.geojson]{.mono} files in [data/raw/shapefiles]{.mono}. *Note: The file ([dc_census.geojson]{.mono} was provided during the problem sets. You may overwrite your existing file.*
    * The file [cicadas_brood_x_2021.csv]{.mono} was provided during the problem sets. Place this in [data/raw]{.mono}. You may overwrite your existing file.
    * Place any R script files ([*.R]) inside of the [scripts]{.mono} folder 
* Run the following to install several new packages!

```{r}
#| eval: false

install.packages(
  c(
    "bench",
    "mapview",
    "rmapshaper",
    "spData",
    "terra"
  )
)
```

***Important!***: Raster functions in the *terra* package will attempt to temporarily store raster files in your computer's memory. If it is unable to do so, it will store the data as a hidden temporary file on your hard drive. Be sure to clear up enough space in your hard disk (at least 5 GB) to complete *terra* operations. If *terra* is unable to store the file, you will get a very vague message about running out of memory (but this message actually has to do with running out of hard disk space).

## About this week's data

This week we will use the following data files in our exercises:

**[canopy_cover.tif]{.mono}**: This is geotiff raster obtained from the [Multi-Resolution Land Characteristics Consortium (MRLC)](https://www.mrlc.gov/data){target="_blank"} that describes the canopy cover in the greater Washington DC region. Cell values are continuous and represent the percentage of each cell that is covered by tree canopy.

**[census ([.dbf]{.mono}, [.prj]{.mono}, [.shp]{.mono}, [.shx]{.mono})]{.mono}**: This is a shapefile from the US Census Bureau that provides tract-level census data for the District of Columbia, Maryland, and Virginia. The data were downloaded using the *tigris* and *tidycensus* packages in R.

**[cicadas_brood_x_2021.csv]{.mono}**: The cicada data is a tabular dataset collected by iNaturalist participants from February through September of 2021 and obtained using the R package *rinat*. The data represent iNaturalist observations of Brood X periodical cicadas from February through September of 2021.

**[counties.geojson]{.mono}**: This is a shapefile of United States counties obtained from the US Census Bureau using the *tigris package*. The resolution of this file is 1:5 million. Each row in the dataset represents a US county.

**[counties_low_res.geojson]{.mono}**: This is a lower resolution (1:20 million) version of the US counties shapefile above. This will be very useful if you have memory or processing limitations on your screen.

**[dc_census.geojson]{.mono}**: This is a shapefile from the US Census Bureau that provides tract-level census data for the District of Columbia. The data were downloaded using the *tigris* and *tidycensus* packages in R.

**[impervious_surface.tif]{.mono}**: This is geotiff raster obtained from the [Multi-Resolution Land Characteristics Consortium (MRLC)](https://www.mrlc.gov/data){target="_blank"} that describes the impervious surface cover in the greater Washington DC region. Cell values are continuous and represent the percentage of each cell that is covered by man-made materials (e.g., pavement, sidewalks, rooftops).

**[nlcd.tif]{.mono}**: This is geotiff raster obtained from the [Multi-Resolution Land Characteristics Consortium (MRLC)](https://www.mrlc.gov/data){target="_blank"} that describes the land cover in the greater Washington DC region. Values are categorical and each value represents the dominant land cover class ([link](https://www.mrlc.gov/data/legends/national-land-cover-database-class-legend-and-description){target="_blank"}) of each cell.

**[rock_creek_park.geojson]{.mono}**: This is a multipolygon shapefile (EPSG 32618; UTM Zone 18N) that represent Washington DC's Rock Creek Park, a National Park that bisects the city.  The data were obtained from [https://opendata.dc.gov/](https://opendata.dc.gov/){target="_blank"}.

**[sick_birds.geojson]{.mono}**: This is a point shapefile that represents sick birds that were brought to City Wildlife, a wildlife rehabilitation center in the District of Columbia, in the spring of 2021. These data were obtained directly from City Wildlife staff.

**[states (.dbf, .prj, .shp, .shx)]{.mono}**: This is shapefile of US states that I obtained from the R package *spData*.

**[Waterbodies_2019.geojson]{.mono}** This is a polygon shapefile (EPSG 4326) that represents surface water in Washington DC.  The data were obtained from [https://opendata.dc.gov/](https://opendata.dc.gov/){target="_blank"}.
